summary: This standards-track RFC clarifies how multiple simultaneous Bidirectional Forwarding Detection sessions are set up, kept running and torn down for a single MPLS label switched path and forwarding equivalence class. It updates RFC 5884 to remove ambiguity that could cause implementations to behave differently.

plainLanguage.summary: Two friends keep checking in with each other to see if the road between them is still open. This clears up the rules for how several check-ins can run at once on the same road.

questions: multiple bfd sessions on one lsp
how do multiple bfd sessions work on one lsp
how are bfd sessions removed at the egress lsr
what is the bfd discriminator tlv
subtitle: Spells out how several BFD liveness sessions can run side by side on one MPLS path, and how they get cleaned up.

tldr.problem: RFC 5884 says several BFD sessions can exist for one MPLS LSP and FEC, but it does not clearly say how to set up, keep or remove them at the same time.
tldr.mechanism: Each LSP ping from the ingress carries a different discriminator, the egress creates a session per new discriminator, and sessions are told apart by the Your Discriminator field. Removal rules are added for the egress.
tldr.outcome: The clarifications are backward compatible with RFC 5884 and can be deployed as a software upgrade. The RFC updates RFC 5884 and has not been obsoleted.

today: RFC 7726 is a Proposed Standard that updates RFC 5884. No later RFC is listed as obsoleting or updating it.

sections.title: Background and Ambiguity in RFC 5884
sections.content:
RFC 5884 defines how to bootstrap and maintain BFD (Bidirectional Forwarding Detection) sessions for an <MPLS LSP, FEC> using an LSP ping. Section 4 of that RFC says multiple BFD sessions can be established for one such tuple, but the procedures for bootstrapping and maintaining them concurrently are not clearly specified. The procedures for removing sessions created on the egress Label Switching Router (LSR) are also unclear.

The RFC names two scenarios where several sessions are useful: LSPs based on Segment Routing and LSPs that use Equal-Cost Multipath (ECMP). How the ingress decides how many sessions to create, and how it builds them, is out of scope.
sections.plainLanguage: An older rulebook said you could have more than one check-in on a road, but it never explained how. This note fills in the missing steps.

sections.title: Establishing Multiple BFD Sessions
sections.content:
RFC 5884 says a BFD session SHOULD be established for each alternate path that is discovered. The ambiguity comes partly from Section 7 of RFC 5884, which forbids either end from changing its local discriminator in BFD control packets once the session is UP. The authors describe the procedures below as their reading of those sections.

At the ingress LSR, MPLS LSP ping can bootstrap multiple BFD sessions for a given <MPLS LSP, FEC>. Each LSP ping MUST carry a different discriminator value in the BFD discriminator TLV.

At the egress LSR, if validation of the FEC in the MPLS Echo request succeeds, it checks the discriminator in the BFD discriminator TLV. If no local session corresponds to that remote discriminator, a new session is bootstrapped and a local discriminator is allocated. Successful FEC validation is necessary to create a session, but any further policy, such as checking system resources, is outside the scope. If policy disallows the session, the egress MUST drop the MPLS Echo request.

The egress must also keep the <MPLS LSP, FEC, Remote Discriminator> tuple unique. The rest of session establishment follows Sections 4 to 6 of RFC 5884.
sections.plainLanguage: Each check-in gets its own name tag. When a new name tag shows up, the other side starts a new check-in for it, unless it is too busy to take on more.

sections.title: Maintaining Sessions with Your Discriminator
sections.content: Once several sessions are running, both the ingress and the egress LSR use the Your Discriminator field of each received BFD packet to demultiplex the sessions, meaning to decide which session the packet belongs to.
sections.plainLanguage: Every message has the name tag of the check-in it belongs to, so each side knows which conversation to put it in.

sections.title: Removing Sessions at the Egress
sections.content:
RFC 5884 gives no explicit procedure for deleting BFD sessions. Removing sessions created by out-of-band discriminator exchange through LSP ping can help resource management, for example memory, when thousands of such sessions exist. The RFC makes several observations.

  • The egress MAY remove a session when it moves from UP to DOWN, either immediately or after a configurable timer that adds hysteresis to reduce flapping.
  • The ingress MAY remove a session on the egress by sending the diagnostic code AdminDown(7) from RFC 5880. To avoid triggering a state change at the egress, it MAY send BFD packets with State Down(1) and diagnostic AdminDown(7) detectMultiplier times, after which the egress MAY remove the session without a state change.
  • What the egress does when sessions stay DOWN for a long time is a local matter.
  • All BFD sessions established with a FEC MUST be removed automatically if the FEC is removed.
  • The egress MUST use the discriminators exchanged when the session came UP to signal any state change, and SHOULD reset them to zero after sending bfd.detectMult packets if the session goes DOWN.
sections.plainLanguage: Old check-ins that nobody needs should be tidied away so they do not clog up memory. Either side can say goodbye politely, and if the road itself is closed, all its check-ins go too.

sections.title: Changing Discriminators
sections.content: The discriminators of a BFD session over an MPLS LSP cannot be changed while it is UP. To use different ones, the session can be removed after a graceful transition to AdminDown using the AdminDown diagnostic code, and a new session established with a different discriminator. Either the ingress or the egress LSR can start the UP to DOWN transition.
sections.plainLanguage: You cannot swap a check-in's name tag in the middle of it. You end it nicely and start a new one with a new tag.

sections.title: Backwards Compatibility
sections.content: The clarified procedures are fully backward compatible with existing implementations of RFC 5884. Current implementations may lack the ability to bootstrap and maintain multiple sessions, but the procedures can be added as a software upgrade without affecting existing sessions. The egress LSR needs to support multiple BFD sessions per <MPLS LSP, FEC> before the ingress LSR is upgraded.
sections.plainLanguage: Nothing that already works breaks. Upgrade the receiving side first, then the sending side.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content: BFD sessions use system and network resources, and more sessions use more. The RFC says it is highly important to provision only the minimum number of sessions per FEC and to delete bootstrapped sessions properly when they are no longer required. The security measures in RFC 4379 and RFC 5884 are still to be followed.
sections.plainLanguage: Too many check-ins waste effort, so only make as many as you need and clean them up afterwards.
